memory_verse: "Conduct yourselves with wisdom toward outsiders, making the most of the opportunity." —Colossians 4:5, NASB

days.focus: Surrendering to God's Love and Asking for Wisdom
days.message_recap: The sermon opened with the promise that believers will bear the image of Christ just as fully as they once bore the image of sinful Adam, and used the image of a criminal surrendering to police to illustrate how God's love — not His threats — compels true surrender. It then turned to Solomon's request for wisdom in 2 Chronicles 1, noting that God commended him for asking for wisdom above all else, and applied this to the believer's task of building God's house today.
days.message_quote: The love of God must—is a Paul said it constrains him. It compelled him. The love of God for Paul became such a powerful force—not the threatening wrath of God, that is also real, but the love of God became such a force to him that he said, 'Lord, I give up. I surrender to You that You would love me so much.'
days.verse_reflection: Colossians 4:5 calls us to walk in wisdom toward those outside the faith, but Romans 8:5-6 makes plain that only those whose minds are set on the Spirit can actually live that way — the flesh-minded person cannot produce the wisdom that outsiders need to see. Ask yourself honestly: in your ordinary interactions this week — at work, at the store, in your home — is your mind genuinely set on the Spirit, or are you relying on natural shrewdness and good manners and calling it wisdom? The fear of God, not social skill, is what makes your conduct among outsiders carry real weight.
days.daily_prayer: Lord, I confess that I have often mistaken a controlled tongue and polite behavior for the wisdom You require. I surrender today — not because I am forced, but because Your love has found me in my hiding place and I have nowhere else to go. Fill me afresh with Your Spirit so that my life among those who do not yet know You is shaped by You alone, and not by what I think will impress them.

days.focus: Christ Crucified as the True Wisdom of God
days.message_recap: The sermon contrasted the earthly wisdom Solomon sought — which ultimately could not keep him from idolatry — with the new covenant wisdom God offers, which is not a body of knowledge but a Person: Christ crucified. Paul's declaration that 'we preach Christ crucified' was presented as the foolishness of God that surpasses all human philosophy and learning, and as the only wisdom that genuinely brings a person into knowing God.
days.message_quote: God is showing us a new wisdom: 'I'm going to show you that wisdom is a Person.' And it's beautiful, in Proverbs 8 you get a little bit of a picture of that. Wisdom is called a Person, she, a Person, and says, 'Before the worlds was created, I was there.'
days.verse_reflection: The memory verse urges wisdom toward outsiders, and Galatians 6:14 shows us what that wisdom is anchored in — the cross of Christ, through which the world has been crucified to Paul and he to the world. True wisdom toward outsiders is not knowing the right thing to say or presenting Christianity attractively; it is living so thoroughly crucified to what the world values — status, comfort, the approval of clever people — that your very life becomes a quiet, unanswerable testimony. Is the cross actually the thing you boast in when you are with people who do not believe, or do you quietly set it aside to seem reasonable?
days.daily_prayer: Father, forgive me for the times I have softened or dressed up the Gospel so that outsiders would find it more acceptable, and in doing so presented a Christ who was not crucified. Let the cross be my only boast today — in my conversations, in what I choose to talk about and what I choose to stay silent about, and in the way I carry myself among those who think it is foolishness. Make me willing to be thought a fool for Your sake.

days.focus: Descending into Nothingness: The Path of True Wisdom
days.message_recap: The sermon walked through 1 Corinthians 1:26-31 to show that God deliberately chooses the foolish, weak, base, despised, and 'things that are not' — a descending progression in the world's eyes — so that no flesh may boast before Him, and that Christ Himself modeled this path by becoming nothing. It then moved into 1 Corinthians 4:10, where Paul says their dedication to Christ makes them look like fools, and challenged listeners to ask whether their own devotion to Christ is radical enough that others would call them fools for it.
days.message_quote: Our dedication to Christ makes us look like fools. Has my dedication and my devotion to Christ made me look like a fool to the rest of the world? 'Santosh, you're a fool. You could do so much more.'
days.verse_reflection: Colossians 4:5 says to make the most of every opportunity with outsiders, but Romans 6:11 shows us the inner condition that makes such opportunity-seizing genuine: reckoning yourself dead to sin and alive to God in Christ. A person who is still very much alive to what others think of them — alive to appearing successful, capable, and impressive — will instinctively use those opportunities with outsiders to manage their image rather than to point to Christ. Examine honestly: when a door opens to speak of Christ to someone today, what is your first instinct — to represent Him clearly, or to represent yourself safely?
days.daily_prayer: Lord, I confess that I am far more alive to the opinions of others than I like to admit, and that this is what makes me hold back from bold witness. I reckon myself dead to that fear today by faith, trusting that You are alive in me. Let my interactions with those outside the faith this week be free from self-protection and full of the foolishness of the cross.

days.focus: Wisdom Comes Through Trials, Not Merely Through Teaching
days.message_recap: The sermon warned against mistaking accumulated Bible knowledge or sermon-listening for genuine wisdom, insisting that true wisdom — which is Christ Himself — can only be received by first acknowledging your lack, then asking God in faith, and then going through the trials God ordains as the means of delivering that wisdom. James 1 was read to show that trials produce endurance, and endurance produces the life that is perfect, complete, and lacking in nothing.
days.message_quote: You acknowledge you lack it, you ask Him, and then He says, 'Okay, I'm going to give it to you, but the way I'm going to give it to you is I'm going to take you through trials.'
days.verse_reflection: The memory verse calls us to walk wisely toward outsiders, but Romans 5:3-5 traces how that kind of seasoned, tested wisdom is actually formed — through tribulation producing perseverance, perseverance producing proven character, and proven character producing hope that does not disappoint. It is easy to be theologically correct about suffering while privately resenting every difficult circumstance that interrupts your plans. Ask yourself: are you treating the trials of this week as inconveniences to escape, or as the very classroom in which God is forming the proven character that will make your witness to outsiders carry genuine weight?
days.daily_prayer: Father, I confess I have often prayed for wisdom while quietly praying against the trials through which You deliver it. I ask You now for wisdom without that contradiction — give me the faith to receive what You are doing in my difficult circumstances this week as Your gift, not Your punishment. Let the endurance You are building in me show itself in how I treat the people around me who are watching.

days.focus: Asking in Faith and the Paradox of Humble Circumstances
days.message_recap: The sermon drew out two conditions for receiving wisdom from James 1: first, genuinely acknowledging your lack and asking God without doubting, since the double-minded person receives nothing; and second, embracing the paradox that the church member in the humblest circumstances holds the highest spiritual position, while the rich person is warned that their visible security will pass away like grass scorched by the sun. The point was that God's economy is the complete inversion of the world's measure of status.
days.message_quote: The brother of humble circumstances is to glory in his high position, and the rich man is to glory in his humiliation, because like flowering grass he will pass away.
days.verse_reflection: Colossians 4:5 calls for wisdom in conduct toward outsiders, and James 4:6 — 'God is opposed to the proud, but gives grace to the humble' — identifies the single inner condition that either opens or closes that channel of wisdom. The person who is quietly proud of their competence, their reputation for handling things well, or even their reputation for being a good witness, is the very person God is actively resisting. It is a searching question: in the specific interactions you are anticipating with unbelievers this week, is there any pride — in how you might come across, in wanting to seem spiritually confident — that is actually blocking the grace you need to walk wisely?
days.daily_prayer: Lord, I humble myself before You right now and acknowledge that I do not have what it takes in myself to walk wisely before those who do not know You. I ask for wisdom without doubting — I choose not to rehearse all the reasons it seems too late or too difficult — and I trust that You give it generously. Strip away any pride that would make You oppose me and replace it with the grace that only comes to the lowly.

days.focus: Wisdom from Above: Pure, Peaceable, and Free from Jealousy
days.message_recap: The sermon turned to James 3 to give the practical proof of heavenly wisdom: it shows itself in gentleness, in freedom from bitter jealousy and selfish ambition, and in a list of qualities — pure, peaceable, gentle, willing to yield, full of mercy, without partiality or hypocrisy — that are the direct opposite of the competitive, self-promoting spirit the world prizes. The preacher warned that jealousy left unchecked is demonic and will produce disorder in a home and family, and called listeners to bring every jealous thought immediately to God as evidence of their need for Christ, who is wisdom.
days.message_quote: When Christ becomes your wisdom, you find this jealousy and selfish ambition goes away. But the wisdom from above — it's pure, it's peaceable, it's gentle, it's willing to yield, full of mercy, and good fruits, not partial, without hypocrisy.
days.verse_reflection: Colossians 4:5 asks us to walk in wisdom toward those outside the faith, and Galatians 5:22-25 shows us that the fruit of the Spirit — love, peace, gentleness, self-control — is exactly the character of that wisdom made visible in ordinary life. The Galatians passage adds a sharp diagnostic: 'those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.' The jealousy and partiality the sermon named are not minor personality quirks — they are works of the flesh, and the only answer is the cross applied daily. Ask yourself honestly: is there anyone in your life — inside the church or outside it — toward whom you feel a flicker of jealousy or competitiveness right now, and are you willing to name it as flesh and bring it to the cross today, rather than justify it?
days.daily_prayer: Lord, I name before You the specific jealousy and selfish ambition I have allowed to remain in my heart, and I ask You to crucify it — not manage it, not suppress it, but put it to death by Your Spirit. Fill that emptiness with the wisdom that comes from above, so that my gentleness and willingness to yield become evident to everyone around me, both those in the church and those still outside of it. Let my conduct toward outsiders this week flow from a heart that is genuinely free, not one that is merely performing.
